items.prompt: Which of these is a business rule?
choices: An order needs at least one line
Connect to the database with a pool
Send the reply as an HTTP 200
items.explanation: A rule is a statement the organization cares about, independent of any tool.

items.prompt: Which of these is infrastructure?
choices: A discount percentage for loyal customers
A database client library
The rule that carts cannot be empty
items.explanation: Database clients, frameworks and queues are tools; the other two are rules.

items.prompt: What makes a rule hard to test in a tangled function?
choices: It is written in too short a function
It uses too many comments
It cannot run without the database
items.explanation: The rule shares a function with the database call, so running one runs both.

items.prompt: In the tangled example, how many of the 40 lines are business rules?
items.explanation: 15 are rules and 25 are plumbing, which is why most of the function is not the point.

items.prompt: What does a test of a tangled rule usually need first?
choices: A second developer to review
A database to be running
A faster computer
items.explanation: The database call is inside the function under test.

items.prompt: Why does swapping the database touch the rule in a tangled design?
choices: Databases always rewrite the rules around them
The rule is stored inside the database itself
The rule's function contains the database calls
items.explanation: They share code, so editing one means editing the other.

items.prompt: Which cost grows with the number of tests?
choices: Setup time for the real database
The number of business rules
The size of the cart
items.explanation: Each test pays the per-test database cost, so the total scales with test count.

items.prompt: Why is a web-framework object inside pricing code a warning sign?
choices: Frameworks are slow to start in most setups
Pricing now depends on a tool unrelated to pricing
Pricing code should always be kept very short
items.explanation: The rule's correctness has nothing to do with how requests arrive.

items.prompt: A suite of 50 tests runs each rule against a real database at an assumed 45 ms each, against 0.05 ms for an in-memory stand-in. What are the two totals?
choices: 2.25 seconds versus 0.0025 seconds, a 900 to 1 gap
2.25 seconds versus 0.025 seconds, a 90 to 1 gap
22.5 seconds versus 0.0025 seconds, a gap of nine thousand
0.45 seconds versus 0.0025 seconds, a gap of 180 to 1
items.explanation: 50 x 45 ms is 2,250 ms, and 50 x 0.05 ms is 2.5 ms. The ratio is 45 / 0.05 = 900, independent of the test count.
items.reference:
Why the tangle hurts
rules: change when the organization changes
infrastructure: changes when a tool or vendor changes
mixed: every rule test pays for the database
assumed cost: 45 ms vs 0.05 ms per test (900 to 1)
Why: separating them lets rules be tested without the slow, fragile parts.
items.learnMore:
Rules and plumbing

A discount rule is correct or not regardless of which database exists. When both live in one function, the rule cannot run without the plumbing, so each test pays setup cost and each tool change risks the rule.

Common mistake

Saying the code is messy. The real problem is the missing seam: nothing separates what changes for business reasons from what changes for tool reasons.
items.reflection: Think of a task at work or home that cannot be tried out without setting up everything around it. What would a seam look like there?

items.prompt: A discount rule is correct, yet its test fails whenever the database container is slow to start. What is the underlying design problem?
choices: The test framework has a timeout set too low
The rule shares a function with the database call
The discount rule should be moved into the database
The database container needs more memory allocated
items.explanation: The failure is about the missing seam. Faster containers hide the symptom but leave the rule unable to run without them.

Rules and persistence were never separated

items.prompt: What is a port?
choices: An interface the core defines for what it needs
A network port number the app listens on for requests
A class that talks to a specific database
items.explanation: A port is the core's description of a need, without saying how it is met.

items.prompt: What is an adapter?
choices: A rule of the business
A concrete implementation of a port
A diagram of the hexagon
items.explanation: Adapters are the technology-specific plugs for the core's sockets.

items.prompt: Which direction do the dependencies point?
choices: Outward, toward the database
Both ways equally
Inward, toward the core
items.explanation: Adapters depend on the core's ports; the core depends on none of them.

items.prompt: Hexagonal and clean architecture are best treated as:
choices: The same pattern in two vocabularies
Two opposed and incompatible designs
A database product and a web framework
items.explanation: Both put rules in a core that outside code plugs into.

items.prompt: Which of these may a core file import?
choices: The database driver
Its own port interfaces
The web framework
items.explanation: Imports of ports keep the core free of technology; the others bind it to a tool.

items.prompt: Which of these is an adapter?
choices: The rule that rejects an empty cart
The OrderRepository interface the core owns
An in-memory order repository for tests
items.explanation: The in-memory repository implements a port with a simple map.

items.prompt: Which principle does this pattern apply at system scale?
choices: Dependency inversion
Single responsibility only
Open for extension only
items.explanation: The core owns the abstraction and details depend on it.

items.prompt: What does swapping Postgres for another store require?
choices: Rewriting the business rules
Writing one new adapter
Changing the port's name
items.explanation: The core only sees the port, so only the plug changes.

items.prompt: A port interface is placed in the Postgres adapter's package, and the core imports it from there. What does that do to the architecture?
choices: The core now imports from the adapter's package, so the dependency points outward
Nothing changes, since an interface is neutral code wherever it sits
The adapter now depends on the core, which is exactly the direction the pattern wants
Compile times improve slightly, and the architecture is otherwise exactly the same as before
items.explanation: Where the interface lives decides who depends on whom. The core importing from the adapter's package reverses the rule even though the type is an interface.
items.reference:
Ports and adapters
core: the rules, no technology imports
port: interface the core owns, says what is needed
adapter: implements a port with a real tool
dependency rule: adapters import the core, never the reverse
Why: the core defines the socket and the outside provides the plug.
items.learnMore:
Ports, adapters, dependency inversion

A port is a socket described in the core's words. An adapter is a plug for one technology. Because the adapter imports the port and not the other way round, the core stays independent of every tool.

Common mistake

Thinking dependencies are inverted just because an interface exists. If the interface lives in the adapter's package or mirrors its API, the core still depends on the technology.
items.reflection: Think of an appliance that works with any wall socket in the world through an adapter. Where would the mismatch land if the appliance depended on one country's socket?

items.prompt: The core's tests need no database, yet two imports from a web framework remain in a core file. What is the accurate conclusion?
choices: The core is fine, because passing tests are what independence means
The core is still coupled to the framework, whatever the passing tests suggest
The framework has become a port, because the core calls it through those imports
The imports are harmless, since code that is never executed cannot create a dependency
items.explanation: The rule is about imports, not test results. A framework import in the core ties it to that tool.

choices: The Postgres adapter importing the core's repository port
The HTTP controller importing the core's use case
A core use case importing the Postgres adapter class
The composition root importing both core and adapters
items.explanation: Only the core-to-adapter import points outward. The other three are adapters or the wiring point importing inward or sideways in permitted ways.

items.prompt: A team calls its design hexagonal because every database call goes through a repository class, but the class returns the ORM's own row objects to the core. What is missing?
choices: A fourth layer between the repository class and the controller
A faster ORM is needed, one with fewer round trips for each of the repository calls
More unit tests are needed for the repository class that wraps the ORM's own calls
The port speaks the ORM's types, so the core still depends on the ORM
items.explanation: Passing ORM types across the boundary pulls the technology into the core. A real port is written in the core's own types.

items.prompt: Which adapter calls into the core?
choices: Primary
Secondary
Neither
items.explanation: Primary adapters drive the core, for example from an HTTP request.

items.prompt: Which is a primary adapter?
choices: A database repository
An HTTP controller
An email sender
items.explanation: The controller receives a request and calls a use case.

items.prompt: Which is a secondary adapter?
choices: A CLI command
A scheduled job
A payment gateway client
items.explanation: The core calls out to it through a port.

items.prompt: A cron job starts a nightly use case. What kind of adapter is it?
choices: Primary
Secondary
A port
items.explanation: It triggers the core, so it drives.

items.prompt: Another word for a primary adapter is:
choices: Driven
Driving
Passive
items.explanation: Driving adapters push into the core.

items.prompt: Another word for a secondary adapter is:
choices: Driving
Triggering
Driven
items.explanation: The core drives them through its ports.

items.prompt: Who defines the interface a secondary adapter implements?
choices: The core
The database vendor
The adapter itself
items.explanation: Ports are owned by the core; adapters conform.

items.prompt: A queue consumer that calls placeOrder for each message is:
choices: Secondary
Primary
Part of the core
items.explanation: Call direction decides, and it calls the core.

items.prompt: A primary adapter's test and a secondary adapter's test ask different questions. Which pairing is right?
choices: Primary: did it turn the trigger into the right core call? Secondary: does it honour the port?
Primary: does it match the port contract? Secondary: did it turn a trigger into a core call?
Both ask whether the real database returns the same stored rows when read back twice in a row
Both ask whether the business rules produce identical totals for the identical inputs every time
items.explanation: Primary adapters are verified on translation into core calls; secondary adapters on satisfying the port the core defined.
items.reference:
Who makes the call
primary (driving): calls into the core
secondary (driven): called by the core through a port
queue worker that triggers a use case: primary
decided by call direction, not by the technology
Why: primary adapters translate triggers; secondary adapters honour contracts.
items.learnMore:
Two families of adapters

A primary adapter turns an outside event into a call on the core, and its test checks that translation. A secondary adapter implements a port the core calls, and its test checks the port's contract.

Common mistake

Sorting by technology. A queue is infrastructure, but a consumer that starts a use case is primary because it calls the core.
items.reflection: Think of a restaurant: customers place orders, and suppliers deliver goods. Which of them call into the kitchen, and which does the kitchen call on?

items.prompt: A new webhook receiver accepts a payment confirmation and calls a core use case. Where does it go?
choices: With the secondary adapters, because payments are external
With the primary adapters, because it calls into the core
Inside the core, since it handles payments
Nowhere, since webhooks are not adapters
items.explanation: It is triggered from outside and invokes the core, so it drives. The topic of the message does not change its direction.

items.prompt: Someone files the email sender under primary adapters because email is a user-facing feature. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Email senders cannot be adapters at all
User-facing features are always secondary
Direction decides: the core calls the sender, so it is secondary
Primary adapters can only ever be web pages, so an email sender cannot be one of them
items.explanation: The sender is invoked by the core through a port. Being user-visible says nothing about who calls whom.

items.prompt: A single class both receives HTTP requests and writes rows to a database. What does the model say about it?
choices: It is a correct secondary adapter, because it writes rows to a database in the end
It is the application core, since it sits between the request and the stored data
It is a port with two methods, one for receiving and one for storing the rows of data
It plays both roles and should be split into one primary and one secondary adapter
items.explanation: Receiving calls and being called through a port are opposite directions. Mixing them recreates the tangle at adapter level.

items.prompt: Who writes a port's method signatures?
choices: The core
The database team
The framework vendor
items.explanation: The core states what it needs; adapters conform.

items.prompt: Which signature is in the core's vocabulary?
choices: executeSql(query)
save(order)
insertRow(table, values)
items.explanation: The first speaks about orders; the others speak about databases.

items.prompt: Why is a SQL string parameter a warning sign on a port?
choices: SQL strings are always too long to type
Strings are impossible to test with a fake
It ties the port to one technology
items.explanation: A fake would have to understand SQL to comply.

items.prompt: Which kind of test double breaks first when a port leaks?
choices: The in-memory fake
The business rule
The composition root
items.explanation: The fake must imitate the leaked technology.

items.prompt: A port is described in terms of:
choices: How the database stores rows
What the core needs
Which driver is installed
items.explanation: The port says what, never how.

items.prompt: Is the port inside or outside the core's code?
choices: Inside the adapter
In the database
Inside, owned by the core
items.explanation: The core owns the interface it depends on.

items.prompt: Who has to adjust when a port changes?
choices: Every adapter implementing it
Only the database it talks to
No one, since ports never change at all
items.explanation: Adapters conform to the port, so they follow it.

items.prompt: Which parameter type belongs on a port?
choices: A vendor query object
A domain object like Order
A connection pool
items.explanation: Domain types keep the port free of tools.

items.prompt: A repository port gains findByRawFilter(filter: string), where the string is a SQL condition. What is the clearest consequence for tests?
choices: The in-memory fake must parse SQL to behave correctly, or it will diverge from Postgres
Nothing changes, because strings are easy to fake
The Postgres adapter can no longer be tested, since raw strings cannot be checked at all
The business rules will run faster
items.explanation: A filter in the database's language forces every implementation to understand that language, defeating the cheap fake.
items.reference:
Port signatures
good: save(order), in the core's vocabulary
leak: save(sqlWhere: string), shaped by Postgres
tell: a fake needs a SQL interpreter to comply
owner: the core, always
Why: if the implementer shapes the port, the dependency has flipped.
items.learnMore:
Ownership of the interface

The core writes the port in the words of the rule that uses it. Adapters then have to fit the socket, not the other way round.

Common mistake

Designing the port around the first adapter's API. It looks convenient, then every later adapter has to imitate that technology.
items.reflection: Think of a standard everyone agreed to plug into. Who gains and who pays when the standard is bent to suit one maker?

items.prompt: Two designs for 'find overdue invoices': findOverdue(asOf: Date) and findWhere(sql: string). Which should the core own, and why?
choices: findWhere, since a raw condition can express every question
findOverdue, because it states the business question and any store can answer it
Both, because offering every possible form of flexibility is always the cheapest long-term choice
Neither, because queries of any kind do not belong behind a port in the first place
items.explanation: A named business question keeps the port stable across stores; a query string hands the shape back to one technology.

items.prompt: A team builds the Postgres adapter first and extracts the port from it afterwards by copying its public methods. What risk does this carry?
choices: The adapter will become slower, as copying methods forces an extra layer of indirection into every call
The core will refuse to compile, because extracted ports cannot be created from existing classes
The port inherits Postgres-specific shapes the core never asked for
The port will contain too few methods, since a public surface hides most of the useful ones
items.explanation: Copying an implementation's surface bakes its quirks into the contract the core must live with.

Ports may take any argument type
The code dependency has quietly flipped, despite what the diagram shows
items.explanation: A vendor type in the signature means the core depends on that vendor, whatever the arrows suggest.

items.prompt: What is the composition root?
choices: The one place where adapters are wired to ports
The root folder of the whole project tree
The main table inside the application database
items.explanation: It builds and connects everything at startup.

items.prompt: Which file is typically the composition root?
choices: A business rule file
main or bootstrap
A test helper only
items.explanation: Startup code is where the wiring belongs.

items.prompt: How many places should construct concrete adapters?
choices: Every use case
One per rule
One
items.explanation: A single place keeps swaps cheap.

items.prompt: May a use case call new on the Postgres adapter?
choices: No
Yes, always
Only in tests
items.explanation: That would import a concrete technology into the core.

items.prompt: Which code may know both ports and concrete adapters?
choices: The business rules of the core
The composition root
The port interfaces themselves
items.explanation: Introducing them is its whole job.

items.prompt: A test wires an in-memory adapter instead of Postgres. What changes?
choices: The use case
The port
Only the wiring
items.explanation: The use case receives whichever adapter it is given.

items.prompt: How does a use case get its adapter?
choices: It is passed in
It looks one up inside
It imports the driver
items.explanation: Passing dependencies in keeps the use case unaware.

items.prompt: What does swapping real email for a fake touch?
choices: Every use case
The composition root
The rules
items.explanation: One wiring edit swaps the adapter.

items.prompt: A use case contains new PostgresOrderRepository(pool) so that callers need not wire anything. What is lost?
choices: The core now names a concrete adapter, so swapping it means editing the core
Nothing is lost, because constructors are cheap and callers no longer need to wire anything up
The ability to run the application at all, since the pool has to be created elsewhere first
The port interface will stop compiling, because a concrete class now sits next to the interface
items.explanation: Convenience was bought by importing the technology into the core, which is what the pattern avoids.
items.reference:
Wiring in one place
composition root: main or bootstrap
knows the ports and every concrete adapter
builds adapters, passes them to use cases
swap = edit one file
Why: construction is concentrated so the core never names a concrete adapter.
items.learnMore:
Where adapters get plugged in

Something has to choose which adapter satisfies each port. Keeping that choice in a single startup file means the rest of the code only sees ports.

Common mistake

Scattering construction around, such as a use case calling `new` on a concrete adapter. That quietly re-imports the technology.
items.reflection: Think of a switchboard where every cable is connected in one room. What would it cost if every office plugged cables in by itself?

items.prompt: An app has 30 use cases and needs to replace one adapter. With a proper composition root, how many files need to change for the swap?
choices: Thirty: each use case
One: the wiring
Two: the port and the adapter's consumer
Zero, since adapters change at runtime
items.explanation: Use cases receive ports; only the place that chooses the adapter changes.

items.learnMore:
Fakes and contract tests

An in-memory adapter makes rule tests fast. A contract suite, written once against the port and run against each adapter, proves the fake and the real adapter behave alike.

Common mistake

Trusting a fake because its own tests pass. Without running the same contract against the real adapter, the two can drift apart unnoticed.

items.learnMore:
Error translation

The port's contract lists which failures can occur in the core's vocabulary. Each adapter catches its technology's exceptions and re-throws those, so the core and its tests never learn driver types.

Common mistake

Letting raw exceptions pass through. It works until the core needs to handle one, and then it imports the driver to name the type.

items.prompt: A team of three builds an internal CRUD form whose only logic is required-field checks. A colleague wants ports for every table. What is the best response?

items.explanation: With no rules to protect, the indirection has nothing to buy. The pattern can be introduced later when logic arrives.
items.reference:
Worth it or not
real rules (pricing, workflow): usually yes
thin CRUD with validation only: usually not
throwaway prototype: not yet
port with one adapter forever: pure overhead
Why: add the seam when logic or testing pain actually shows up.
items.learnMore:
Cost versus value

The pattern costs files, interfaces and a wiring point. It pays back when there are rules worth testing cheaply or a real second implementation, a test double included.

Common mistake

Applying it everywhere by habit. A port that will only ever have one adapter returns nothing for its indirection.

items.prompt: Does hiding the database behind a port make two writes atomic?
choices: No
Yes
Only in tests
items.explanation: Atomicity needs a transaction strategy, not just an abstraction.

items.prompt: What is a unit of work?
choices: A single test that checks one rule
One commit wrapping several operations
A kind of adapter used for sending email
items.explanation: It groups operations so they succeed or fail together.

items.prompt: Which strategy suits two writes in one database?
choices: A compensating action only
Ignoring failures
A shared transaction
items.explanation: One database can commit both together.

items.prompt: What is a compensating action?
choices: An undo that runs when a later step fails
A faster way to commit a transaction
A retry of the first step in the sequence
items.explanation: It repairs state without a shared transaction.

items.prompt: Order saved, stock not decremented. What went wrong?
choices: The port was too small for the job
The two steps were not atomic
The business rule itself was wrong
items.explanation: The first step succeeded and the second failed.

items.prompt: If stock lives in another service, can one database transaction cover both?
choices: Yes
Only on Tuesdays
No
items.explanation: A transaction cannot span different systems.

items.prompt: Which gives a single boundary over two operations in one store?
choices: A combined adapter
Two unrelated adapters
A bigger test
items.explanation: One adapter can own one transaction.

items.prompt: Which systems units cover the deeper mechanics?
choices: Naming and logging
Transactions and race conditions
Color and typography
items.explanation: They handle atomicity and concurrency.

items.prompt: Saving an order and decrementing stock must succeed together, and both live in the same database. Which design fits best?
choices: A unit of work port, or a single adapter, that owns one transaction
Two independent ports that each commit on their own right after their own write succeeds
A compensating action sent after the second write fails
A retry loop around the second call
items.explanation: Same database means a real transaction is available, so use it instead of repairing afterwards.
items.reference:
Atomicity across ports
unit of work port: one commit for several operations
one combined adapter: single transaction
compensating action: undo if step two fails
different systems: compensation is all that remains
Why: a port hides the technology; it does not make two writes succeed together.
items.learnMore:
Atomic boundaries

Two ports can each work correctly and still leave the system half-done if the second fails. Atomicity needs an explicit strategy chosen to fit where the data actually lives.

Common mistake

Assuming the abstraction implies a transaction. Hiding Postgres behind a port does not make two calls commit together.
items.reflection: Think of paying a deposit and booking a venue with two separate offices. What would make you whole if one of them says no?

Make the port retry until the service answers
items.explanation: A local transaction cannot reach another system. The saved order must be undone or marked after the fact.
